  • Connect decisions to reliability, maintainability, and delivery speed.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Define constraints and target outcomes clearly.
  • Explain tradeoffs and alternatives.
  • Connect decisions to reliability, maintainability, and delivery speed.

docs.title: Cancellation and exception handling
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Cancellation and Exception Handling Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Cancellation and exception propagation are where coroutine understanding becomes production-relevant.

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text: Coroutine cancellation is cooperative. It works well when code reaches suspension points or checks cancellation explicitly.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Exception behavior depends on:

  • coroutine builder (launch vs async)
  • parent-child hierarchy
  • supervisor boundaries
  • where exceptions are observed

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Cancellation is represented by job state changes and propagated through job hierarchy.

A coroutine that never suspends or checks cancellation may continue running longer than expected.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Suspend functions cooperate with cancellation through coroutine machinery, not through thread interruption alone.

CoroutineExceptionHandler is only for uncaught exceptions; it is not a general substitute for structured error handling.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
while (isActive) {
    doWorkChunk()
}

try {
    doWork()
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is cancellation called cooperative?
  • Why should CancellationException usually be rethrown?
  • Why doesn't CoroutineExceptionHandler catch everything?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Common bugs:

  • swallowing cancellation accidentally
  • blocking threads inside coroutines
  • assuming try/catch and handler behavior are identical across builders

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Cancellation responsiveness matters for UI, battery, and resource cleanup. Poor cancellation behavior can waste work and degrade UX.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Good coroutine engineers think about cancellation and exception strategy during API design, not only when debugging failures.

docs.title: Collections and sequences
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kotlin collections are highly expressive, but interview discussions often focus on eagerness, allocation behavior, and immutability semantics.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Common operations:

  • map
  • filter
  • flatMap
  • groupBy
  • associate

Key nuance:

  • List<T> is read-only from that API surface
  • it is not necessarily deeply immutable

Sequences differ because they are lazy.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Collection chains usually allocate intermediate collections. Sequence chains defer work and process lazily.

That means sequences can reduce allocations, but also add iterator/lazy overhead.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text: The compiler does not magically optimize every chain away. Standard library operations still correspond to loops, lambdas, and allocated containers depending on API choice.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val names = users
    .filter { it.active }
    .map { it.name }

val names = users.asSequence()
    .filter { it.active }
    .map { it.name }
    .toList()

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• When should you use Sequence?
  • Are Kotlin collections immutable?
  • Why can operator chains become allocation-heavy?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Use collection chains for readable business logic. Switch to sequences only when dataset size and allocation pressure justify it.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
• small collections: eager collections are often fine
  • large pipelines: sequences may help
  • hot paths: benchmark rather than assume

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong answers avoid blanket rules like “Sequence is always faster.” Context matters.

docs.title: Coroutines foundations
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kotlin coroutines provide a structured, lightweight way to write asynchronous code in a sequential style.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Core building blocks:

  • suspend functions
  • CoroutineScope
  • CoroutineContext
  • Job
  • Dispatcher

Coroutines are not threads. They are units of work scheduled onto threads.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Suspend functions compile into continuation-passing style. The compiler transforms suspend code into resumable state machines.

At a high level, the transformation adds:

  • a continuation parameter
  • labels/states
  • logic for resuming from suspension points

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
A suspend function is not just “async syntax.” It becomes lower-level machinery that coordinates with Continuation objects and resumable state transitions.

This is one of the most important advanced Kotlin interview topics.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
suspend fun fetchUser(): User {
    delay(100)
    return User("1")
}

Conceptually, the compiler rewrites this into a resumable form rather than a simple blocking method.

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Does suspend mean background thread?
  • What is a continuation?
  • How are coroutines lighter than threads?
  • What does CPS transformation mean?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Coroutines simplify async logic, but misuse can still cause:

  • lifecycle leaks
  • wrong dispatcher use
  • hidden cancellation bugs
  • unstructured work

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Coroutines are cheaper than threads, but not free. Large numbers of coroutines still create scheduling and allocation overhead.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
The strongest interview answers explain coroutines at both levels:

  • high-level developer ergonomics
  • low-level compiler/runtime model

docs.title: Data classes and generated code
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Data Classes and Generated Code Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Data classes are Kotlin's value-oriented modeling tool. They remove boilerplate while making equality, debugging, and copying semantics explicit.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
A data class is best when the object primarily represents data rather than identity-heavy behavior.

data class User(
    val id: Long,
    val name: String
)

Kotlin generates:

  • equals()
  • hashCode()
  • toString()
  • copy()
  • componentN()

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
The compiler only uses properties in the primary constructor for generated member behavior.

data class Session(val token: String) {
    var isExpired: Boolean = false
}

Here:

  • token participates in equality/hash/copy
  • isExpired does not

That is an important interview trap.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Kotlin data classes compile to normal JVM classes with generated methods.

Conceptually, the compiler emits methods similar to:

override fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean
override fun hashCode(): Int
override fun toString(): String
fun copy(id: Long = this.id, name: String = this.name): User
operator fun component1(): Long
operator fun component2(): String

Default arguments in copy() also generate additional helper methods on JVM.

docs.title: Copying immutable state
docs.text:
data class UiState(
    val loading: Boolean,
    val title: String
)

val oldState = UiState(loading = true, title = "Home")
val newState = oldState.copy(loading = false)

docs.title: Destructuring
docs.text:
val user = User(1L, "Mina")
val (id, name) = user

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What gets included in generated equality?
  • Is a data class automatically immutable?
  • Why is copy() useful in Android UI state?
  • When should you avoid data classes?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use data classes for:

  • UI state
  • API models
  • cached domain values
  • immutable state containers

Avoid overusing them for objects with strong identity/lifecycle semantics.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Data classes are usually efficient enough, but beware of:

  • repeated copy() on large nested graphs
  • accidental deep-state churn in UI reducers
  • large generated toString() logs in hot paths

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
The strongest interview answers distinguish:

  • value semantics vs identity semantics
  • generated convenience vs real allocation cost
  • immutable state modeling vs mutable entities

That distinction matters heavily in Android architecture and state management.

docs.title: Delegation and delegated properties
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Delegation and Delegated Properties Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Delegation is one of Kotlin's strongest language features for reducing boilerplate and favoring composition.

docs.title: Class delegation
docs.text:
interface Printer {
    fun print()
}

class ConsolePrinter : Printer {
    override fun print() = println("print")
}

class Screen(printer: Printer) : Printer by printer

This forwards interface implementation automatically.

docs.title: Property delegation
docs.text:
val config by lazy { loadConfig() }

The delegate owns access behavior.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Delegated properties are compiled into calls to delegate operators such as:

  • getValue()
  • setValue()

Class delegation similarly becomes generated forwarding methods.

So Kotlin removes boilerplate, but the underlying implementation still uses regular method calls and generated glue.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
lazy uses a delegate implementation chosen by thread-safety mode.

Common modes:

  • synchronized (default)
  • publication
  • none

This matters in interview discussions because “lazy” behavior is not one-size-fits-all.

docs.title: lazy
docs.text:
val repository by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) {
    UserRepository()
}

docs.title: Observable property
docs.text:
var count: Int by Delegates.observable(0) { _, old, new ->
    println("$old -> $new")
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is delegation better than inheritance here?
  • How does lazy behave with threads?
  • What methods must a custom delegate implement?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Delegation is excellent for:

  • reusable behaviors
  • view binding style patterns
  • state observation
  • lightweight wrappers

But hidden magic can hurt readability if overused.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Delegation reduces manual boilerplate but still introduces generated calls. In most app code the clarity benefit outweighs the tiny indirection cost.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong candidates explain delegation as a language-supported composition mechanism, not just “syntactic sugar.” That distinction matters in architecture discussions.

docs.title: Dispatchers and coroutine scope
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Dispatchers and Coroutine Scope Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Dispatchers and scopes determine where coroutines run and who owns their lifetime.

docs.title: Dispatchers
docs.text:
• Main → UI thread
  • IO → blocking I/O work
  • Default → CPU-heavy work
  • Unconfined → special-case behavior, rarely appropriate in app code

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text: A CoroutineScope defines the lifecycle boundary for its coroutines.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Dispatchers are elements of coroutine context. Scopes combine context plus job hierarchy rules.

The important concept is that execution context and ownership travel together through coroutine context composition.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Dispatchers do not change what coroutines are. They change scheduling and thread execution behavior.

withContext(...) is commonly used to switch execution context safely.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
viewModelScope.launch {
    val result = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        repository.fetch()
    }
    render(result)
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What is the difference between scope and dispatcher?
  • Why is Dispatchers.IO different from Default?
  • Why is GlobalScope discouraged?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use lifecycle-aware scopes on Android:

  • viewModelScope
  • lifecycleScope

Avoid unowned coroutine launches unless there is a very explicit reason.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Wrong dispatcher selection can cause:

  • blocked UI
  • thread starvation
  • wasted parallelism
  • poor responsiveness

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior-level answers connect dispatcher choice to workload type and connect scope choice to ownership and cancellation boundaries.

docs.title: Extension functions
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Extension functions make Kotlin APIs feel richer without modifying original classes.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
fun String.firstCharOrNull(): Char? = firstOrNull()

This reads like a member call:

val c = "Kotlin".firstCharOrNull()

But extension functions do not actually inject members into the class.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Extensions are compiled as static-like functions with the receiver passed as an argument.

That is why extension dispatch is static, not virtual.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Key interview rules:

  • receiver is just a parameter at compile time
  • member functions beat extensions if signatures match
  • runtime subtype does not change extension resolution
open class A
class B : A()

fun A.label() = "A"
fun B.label() = "B"

val value: A = B()
println(value.label()) // "A"

docs.title: Android-flavored helper
docs.text:
fun TextView.showIf(condition: Boolean) {
    visibility = if (condition) View.VISIBLE else View.GONE
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Are extension functions polymorphic?
  • Do they really modify the original class?
  • When should you prefer extension functions over utility objects?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use extensions for:

  • readable helpers
  • framework convenience APIs
  • DSL-like builders

Avoid putting too much business logic in obscure extension files.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Extensions usually have no special runtime magic beyond regular function calls unless combined with inline.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Extension functions are great API design tools, but poor organization can make code discovery harder. Keep naming and file placement disciplined.

docs.title: Flow fundamentals
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Flow is Kotlin's coroutine-based asynchronous stream API and a core part of modern Android data pipelines.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Key properties of Flow:

  • cold by default
  • sequential by default
  • cancellation-aware
  • coroutine based

A cold stream starts producing values for each collector independently.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
A flow builder defines a suspendable emission pipeline. Collection triggers execution.

That means a Flow is closer to a reusable recipe for producing values than a constantly running producer.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text: Flow sits on top of coroutines and suspend machinery. Many operators are implemented as chains of suspendable transformations.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
fun userFlow(): Flow<User> = flow {
    emit(loadUser())
}

viewModelScope.launch {
    userFlow().collect { user ->
        render(user)
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What does “cold” mean in Flow?
  • How is Flow different from LiveData or Rx streams?
  • Why is Flow sequential by default?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Flow is powerful for:

  • repository streams
  • UI state pipelines
  • database observation
  • combining async sources

But careless operator chains and repeated collections can create inefficiency.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Understand:

  • collection triggers execution
  • repeated collectors repeat cold work
  • buffering/concurrency operators affect throughput and ordering

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: The strongest answers explain Flow not just as “reactive streams,” but as coroutine-native cold stream pipelines with explicit lifecycle and collection semantics.

docs.title: Generics and variance
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kotlin generics improve type safety, but their most important interview topics are variance and type erasure.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Generics let APIs work across different types safely:

class Box<T>(val value: T)

Variance controls subtype relationships:

  • out = producer
  • in = consumer

Star projection (*) represents an unknown type argument safely.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
On JVM, generic type arguments are largely erased at runtime. That means many generic guarantees exist mainly at compile time.

This is why runtime checks and reified solutions matter.

docs.title: Covariance
docs.text: interface Source<out T>

docs.title: Contravariance
docs.text: interface Consumer<in T>

docs.title: Star projection
docs.text:
val list: List<*> = listOf("a", "b")

Kotlin avoids Java-style raw type ambiguity by making unknown generic usage safer.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
fun copyAll(from: List<out Number>, to: MutableList<in Number>) {
    from.forEach { to.add(it) }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• What is variance?
  • What is the producer/consumer rule?
  • Why does type erasure matter?
  • Why is List<String> not automatically List<Any>?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Variance improves API correctness, especially in libraries and architecture boundaries. Poor variance choices can make APIs painful or unsafe.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: The main cost is not performance but complexity. The challenge is making APIs type-safe without making them unreadable.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
Strong answers connect generic theory to real API design:

  • safe library surfaces
  • better abstraction boundaries
  • reduced casting
  • more predictable contracts

docs.title: Higher order functions and lambdas
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Higher-Order Functions and Lambdas Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Higher-order functions are central to idiomatic Kotlin API design. They power collection transformations, builders, coroutines, Flow, and DSLs.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
A higher-order function either:

  • accepts a function
  • returns a function
fun repeat(times: Int, block: () -> Unit) {
    kotlin.repeat(times) { block() }
}

Lambda with receiver example:

fun buildMessage(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String {
    return StringBuilder().apply(block).toString()
}

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Lambdas can compile into:

  • generated classes/objects
  • inlined code when used with inline functions

Lambdas with receiver are still function types, but with an implicit receiver available inside the body.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Without inlining, lambdas may allocate objects. With inline functions, the compiler can reduce or remove that overhead.

This is why Kotlin's higher-order style is expressive but still tied to JVM allocation and bytecode tradeoffs.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val doubled = listOf(1, 2, 3).map { it * 2 }

val text = buildMessage {
    append("Hello ")
    append("Kotlin")
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why are higher-order functions important in Kotlin?
  • What is a lambda with receiver?
  • How do inline functions affect lambda cost?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Use higher-order APIs to improve abstraction and reuse, but avoid creating APIs so abstract that they become hard to debug.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Main cost areas:

  • lambda allocation
  • capturing outer variables
  • deep operator chains

These matter most in hot paths.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: The best Kotlin APIs often feel declarative because of higher-order functions, but strong engineers balance API elegance with debuggability and runtime cost.

docs.title: Inline functions
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Inline functions are a compiler-level optimization and language feature used heavily with Kotlin lambdas and reified generics.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
inline fun measure(block: () -> Unit) {
    val start = System.nanoTime()
    block()
    println(System.nanoTime() - start)
}

Inlining means the function body may be copied into the call site.

Benefits:

  • fewer lambda allocations
  • fewer function call boundaries
  • support for non-local returns in inline lambdas

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
The compiler substitutes the inline function body directly into call sites when possible.

This is why:

  • reified type parameters work
  • non-local returns become possible
  • bytecode can grow if abused

docs.title: noinline
docs.text: Prevents a specific lambda from being inlined.

docs.title: crossinline
docs.text:
Allows inlining but forbids non-local return.

These exist because not all lambda usages can be inlined safely or semantically.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
inline fun runner(block: () -> Unit) {
    block()
}

inline fun wrapper(crossinline block: () -> Unit) {
    val r = Runnable { block() }
    r.run()
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why are inline functions useful for higher-order APIs?
  • When do they hurt performance?
  • Why does reified require inline?
  • What do crossinline and noinline solve?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Inline small, hot higher-order utilities. Avoid inlining large bodies blindly.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Inlining can remove overhead, but can also increase:

  • bytecode size
  • method complexity
  • instruction cache pressure

It is a targeted optimization, not a blanket rule.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
Good interview answers connect inline functions to:

  • bytecode tradeoffs
  • lambda allocation behavior
  • API ergonomics
  • reified generics support

docs.title: Jvm interop and bytecode
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: JVM Interop and Bytecode Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Kotlin is deeply integrated with the JVM. Understanding interop and bytecode helps explain how Kotlin features behave in real Android codebases.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Important interop topics:

  • calling Java from Kotlin
  • exposing Kotlin to Java
  • nullability differences
  • default arguments
  • companion/static-like APIs
  • SAM conversions

Important bytecode topics:

  • generated helper methods
  • lambda classes
  • null checks
  • suspend state machines
  • inline expansion

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Many Kotlin features are compiler conveniences over regular JVM structures.

Examples:

  • default arguments generate helper methods
  • top-level declarations compile into generated holder classes
  • suspend functions add continuation machinery

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Kotlin source can look very high-level, but the emitted bytecode still follows JVM constraints.

That is why knowledge of:

  • type erasure
  • generated methods
  • interop annotations
  • bytecode layout

makes interview answers much stronger.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
class UserFactory {
    companion object {
        @JvmStatic
        fun create() = UserFactory()
    }
}

inline fun <reified T> check(value: Any) = value is T

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• How does Kotlin handle Java nullability?
  • What does @JvmStatic do?
  • Why does Kotlin generate extra methods?
  • How do suspend functions appear in bytecode?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Interop bugs often happen at boundaries:

  • Java APIs with unclear nullability
  • default args exposed poorly to Java
  • reflection/serialization expectations
  • method count and generated helper complexity

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Bytecode awareness helps explain:

  • method growth
  • allocation behavior
  • lambda overhead
  • inlining tradeoffs

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior candidates stand out when they connect Kotlin language ergonomics to emitted JVM artifacts and operational consequences.

docs.title: Kotlin basics
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Kotlin is a modern statically typed language that runs primarily on the JVM and was designed to improve safety, expressiveness, and developer productivity.

For Android interviews, Kotlin basics are not just syntax questions. Interviewers often expect you to connect Kotlin language design to:

  • safer APIs
  • fewer runtime crashes
  • clearer state modeling
  • better interop with Java
  • reduced boilerplate in Android apps

docs.title: Why Kotlin became the Android default
docs.text:
Kotlin fits Android well because it improves several pain points from Java-heavy Android codebases:

  • null handling is explicit in the type system
  • common patterns require less code
  • lambdas and extension functions make APIs cleaner
  • coroutines improve async programming ergonomics
  • interoperability lets teams adopt it incrementally

docs.title: val vs var
docs.text:
val name = "Kotlin"
var count = 0
  • val = reference cannot be reassigned
  • var = reference can be reassigned

Important nuance:

val items = mutableListOf("a")
items.add("b") // valid
// items = mutableListOf() // invalid

So val gives a stable reference, not automatic deep immutability.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
From a compiler perspective, Kotlin basics still map to regular JVM concepts:

  • top-level functions become static-like methods in generated classes
  • properties compile into fields/getters/setters depending on usage
  • val often becomes a field with getter only
  • var usually becomes a field with both getter and setter

The surface syntax is cleaner, but the generated model is still understandable from a JVM point of view.

docs.title: Property generation
docs.text:
class User {
    val id: Int = 1
    var name: String = "A"
}

This generally compiles into:

  • backing fields when needed
  • getId()
  • getName()
  • setName()

Interview insight: Kotlin language features often look new, but many are compiler conveniences over classic bytecode patterns.

docs.title: Prefer val by default
docs.text:
val repository = UserRepository()
val users = repository.loadUsers()

docs.title: Use var only when mutation is real and local
docs.text:
var retries = 0
while (retries < 3) {
    retries++
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is val preferred over var?
  • Does val mean immutable object?
  • What does Kotlin compile to on the JVM?
  • Why is Kotlin safer than Java in practice?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• prefer immutable modeling for UI state
  • keep mutation local and obvious
  • use Kotlin features to improve maintainability, not cleverness
  • avoid excessive nesting of idiomatic helpers if readability drops

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Basic Kotlin syntax itself is not usually the bottleneck.

The real performance questions come from:

  • allocation patterns
  • lambdas and closures
  • inlining
  • collection transformations
  • coroutine usage

So Kotlin basics matter more for correctness and readability than raw speed.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
Strong Kotlin interview answers connect language fundamentals to engineering tradeoffs:

  • val improves reasoning about state
  • explicit nullability improves API contracts
  • better syntax can reduce bug surface area
  • compiler-generated convenience still has JVM cost and structure

The best answers show both language fluency and runtime awareness.

docs.title: Null safety and smart casts
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Null Safety and Smart Casts Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Null safety is one of Kotlin's biggest value propositions. It moves many null-related problems from runtime into the type system.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Kotlin distinguishes:

  • String → non-nullable
  • String? → nullable

Main tools:

  • safe call ?.
  • Elvis ?:
  • not-null assertion !!
  • smart casts after checks

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Kotlin null safety is mostly compiler enforced. The type system tracks nullable vs non-nullable references and emits checks where needed.

Platform types from Java weaken these guarantees because nullability may be unknown at compile time.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
The compiler often inserts runtime null-checks for parameters and assumptions, especially around Java interop and non-null contracts.

Smart casts rely on flow analysis. They work only when the compiler can prove the reference is stable.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val name: String? = input()
val length = name?.length ?: 0

if (value is String) {
    println(value.length) // smart cast
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why can null still happen in Kotlin?
  • What is a platform type?
  • When do smart casts fail?
  • Why is !! dangerous?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• avoid !! unless failure is intentional
  • make nullability explicit in public APIs
  • be careful at Java boundaries
  • prefer safe transformations to assertions

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Null safety is primarily a correctness feature. Runtime cost is usually minor compared with the stability benefit.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Good candidates explain that Kotlin reduces null problems significantly, but cannot eliminate them when unsafe assertions, Java interop, reflection, or poor API design are involved.

docs.title: Object and companion objects
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Object and Companion Objects Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text:
Kotlin's object keyword covers several patterns:

  • singleton declarations
  • anonymous object expressions
  • companion objects

Interviewers often test whether you understand both the syntax and the runtime differences.

docs.title: Object declaration
docs.text:
object Logger {
    fun log(message: String) = println(message)
}
  • named singleton
  • lazily initialized on first access
  • useful for stateless shared utilities

docs.title: Object expression
docs.text:
val listener = object : Runnable {
    override fun run() = println("run")
}
  • anonymous object
  • created immediately
  • often used for local callbacks

docs.title: Companion object
docs.text:
class User {
    companion object {
        const val TABLE = "users"
    }
}
  • tied to a class
  • often used for factories/constants
  • Kotlin alternative to many Java static use cases

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Companion objects are still real objects. They are not magical static blocks.

That means they can:

  • implement interfaces
  • hold state
  • contain functions
  • be referenced as objects
class FactoryHolder {
    companion object Factory : Comparator<Int> {
        override fun compare(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a - b
    }
}

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
On JVM, Kotlin often generates a companion instance field plus methods.

With annotations like @JvmStatic, interop can become more Java-friendly.

Interview nuance:

  • companion objects are object instances
  • Java statics are class-level members
  • the call style may look similar, but the compiled model differs

docs.title: Factory pattern
docs.text:
class User private constructor(val id: Long) {
    companion object {
        fun fromId(id: Long): User = User(id)
    }
}

docs.title: Anonymous object for one-off behavior
docs.text:
fun makeRunnable(): Runnable {
    return object : Runnable {
        override fun run() = println("working")
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Is a companion object the same as static?
  • When is an object declaration initialized?
  • What is lost when returning an anonymous object from a public API?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use object declarations for:

  • stateless helpers
  • shared formatters
  • singleton configuration readers

Avoid hidden global mutable state unless truly necessary.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: The main concern is usually not speed but initialization and hidden state. Singleton misuse can quietly turn into global coupling.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
Strong answers emphasize:

  • object forms model different intent
  • companion objects are still objects
  • singletons simplify access but can hurt testability if overused

docs.title: Reified generics
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Reified generics are one of Kotlin's most interview-worthy features because they connect language syntax to JVM type erasure and compiler inlining.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Normally, JVM generics are erased at runtime.

Kotlin solves some of that limitation with reified type parameters in inline functions:

inline fun <reified T> Any.isType(): Boolean = this is T

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Because the function is inlined, the compiler can substitute real type checks at the call site.

That is why this is possible only inside inline functions.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
Without reified support, this is not possible safely:

fun <T> check(value: Any): Boolean {
    // cannot use `is T` here normally
    return false
}

With reified:

inline fun <reified T> check(value: Any): Boolean = value is T

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJsonTyped(json: String): T {
    return fromJson(json, T::class.java)
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why does reified require inline?
  • How does it relate to type erasure?
  • When is reified more useful than reflection?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text: Reified generics improve API ergonomics, but still depend on JVM/runtime limits. They are especially useful for utility libraries and framework helpers.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: The main tradeoff is still inline-related bytecode duplication, not magic runtime cost.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong answers connect reified generics to compiler substitution, not just “Kotlin can access generic types at runtime.” The mechanism matters.

docs.title: Scope functions
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Scope functions help structure object-centric code, but their real interview value is understanding tradeoffs, not memorizing a chart.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Main functions:

  • let
  • run
  • with
  • apply
  • also

They differ by:

  • receiver style (this vs it)
  • return type (receiver vs lambda result)

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text: Scope functions are just normal library functions. There is no special runtime scope feature; readability comes from how the compiler resolves receivers and lambda parameters.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text: At bytecode level, these become regular function calls/lambda invocations. The complexity is mainly cognitive, not magical.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val length = name?.let { it.trim().length }

val user = User().apply {
    id = 1
    name = "Mina"
}

logger.also {
    println("created")
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Which scope function returns the receiver?
  • Which one is best for null-safe transforms?
  • Why can overusing scope functions hurt readability?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Good uses:

  • object setup with apply
  • null-safe transforms with let
  • side-effect logging with also

Bad uses:

  • deeply nested chained scopes
  • mixing multiple implicit receivers carelessly

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Performance differences are usually minor. Readability and maintainability matter more.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Senior engineers choose scope functions intentionally. The best code often uses fewer of them, not more.

docs.title: Sealed classes and enums
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Sealed Classes and Enums Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Sealed classes and enum classes both model limited domains, but they solve different problems.

docs.title: Enum classes
docs.text:
Best for a fixed set of singleton constants.

enum class SortOrder {
    ASCENDING,
    DESCENDING
}

docs.title: Sealed classes
docs.text:
Best for closed hierarchies where each case may carry different data.

sealed class UiState {
    object Loading : UiState()
    data class Success(val items: List<String>) : UiState()
    data class Error(val message: String) : UiState()
}

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Enums create one instance per enum constant. Sealed classes define a restricted inheritance tree.

Key difference:

  • enum = fixed constants
  • sealed = fixed subtype set

That makes sealed classes much stronger for state/result/event modeling.

docs.title: Enums
docs.text: Compile to Java-style enum classes with constant instances.

docs.title: Sealed classes
docs.text:
Compile as regular classes/interfaces with metadata allowing the compiler to reason about exhaustiveness.

The JVM itself does not “understand” sealed behavior the same way Kotlin source does; much of the experience is compiler driven.

docs.title: Exhaustive when
docs.text:
fun render(state: UiState): String = when (state) {
    UiState.Loading -> "loading"
    is UiState.Success -> state.items.joinToString()
    is UiState.Error -> state.message
}

docs.title: Enum use case
docs.text:
enum class ThemeMode {
    LIGHT,
    DARK,
    SYSTEM
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• When should you choose sealed over enum?
  • Why is sealed useful for UI state?
  • Does sealed always mean no else in when?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use enums for:

  • simple flags
  • static modes
  • limited status values

Use sealed classes for:

  • state machines
  • result wrappers
  • navigation outcomes
  • view state models

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: The choice is usually more about modeling clarity than raw performance. But sealed class instances can allocate more frequently if used carelessly in high-frequency state updates.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
The best modeling tool is the one that matches the domain:

  • enum for simple symbolic constants
  • sealed for structured closed-state systems

That distinction improves both correctness and maintainability.

docs.title: Stateflow sharedflow and channels
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: StateFlow, SharedFlow, and Channels Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: These primitives solve different streaming and coordination problems in coroutine-based systems.

docs.title: StateFlow
docs.text:
• always has a current value
  • best for state exposure
  • good for UI state models

docs.title: SharedFlow
docs.text:
• hot broadcast stream
  • configurable replay/buffering
  • good for events/shared emissions

docs.title: Channel
docs.text:
• point-to-point communication primitive
  • queue-like semantics
  • send/receive model

docs.title: Mutex
docs.text:
• protects shared mutable state cooperatively
  • suspends instead of blocking threads

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
These primitives differ in ownership and delivery semantics:

  • state retention (StateFlow)
  • broadcast fan-out (SharedFlow)
  • queue handoff (Channel)
  • mutual exclusion (Mutex)

Interviewers often care more about correct use-case matching than API memorization.

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text: All of them are coroutine/runtime constructs, not magical language features. Their behavior emerges from concurrency contracts and buffering rules.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
private val _state = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state

private val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>()

val mutex = Mutex()
mutex.withLock {
    updateSharedState()
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• StateFlow vs SharedFlow?
  • Channel vs SharedFlow?
  • When use Mutex instead of synchronized locking?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Common mistakes:

  • using StateFlow for one-off UI events
  • using channels where broadcast behavior is needed
  • ignoring replay/buffer semantics
  • mutating shared state without synchronization

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
Hot stream choice affects:

  • memory retention
  • buffering pressure
  • event loss or duplication
  • collector coordination cost

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: Strong engineers choose these primitives based on delivery semantics and lifecycle guarantees, not habit.

docs.title: Structured concurrency and jobs
docs.text: ← Back to Kotlin

docs.title: Structured Concurrency and Jobs Deep Dive
Overview
docs.text: Structured concurrency gives coroutine trees clear ownership and predictable lifecycle behavior.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
In structured concurrency:

  • coroutines are launched in a scope
  • parent-child relationships are explicit
  • parents usually wait for children
  • cancellation and failure have defined propagation rules

Job represents coroutine lifecycle. SupervisorJob changes failure propagation semantics.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
Each coroutine context usually includes a Job element. Child jobs attach to parent jobs to build a hierarchy.

This hierarchy powers:

  • cancellation propagation
  • completion coordination
  • structured waiting

docs.title: JVM / Compiler Behavior
docs.text:
This is not just syntax style. The runtime job tree controls actual coroutine lifecycle behavior.

That is why launch, async, Job, and SupervisorJob matter beyond API surface.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
coroutineScope {
    launch { workA() }
    launch { workB() }
}

val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main)

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Why is structured concurrency safer than ad-hoc launching?
  • What is the difference between Job and SupervisorJob?
  • When should you use async instead of launch?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
Use structured concurrency to avoid:

  • leaked work
  • orphan background jobs
  • unpredictable cancellation behavior

This is especially important in Android lifecycle-bound scopes.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text: Structured concurrency is mainly about correctness and maintainability, but it also improves debuggability and reduces accidental runaway work.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: The best answers explain job hierarchy as an ownership model, not just an API detail. That framing is what interviewers often want.

docs.title: Api versioning scalability
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: API versioning enables evolution. CDN scales static assets.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Versioning strategies: 1. Path: /v1/users 2. Header: Accept: application/vnd.api+v2 3. Query: /users?version=2 CDN caches static globally.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// Retrofit with version header
val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addNetworkInterceptor { chain ->
        val request = chain.request().newBuilder()
            .addHeader("API-Version", "2")
            .build()
        chain.proceed(request)
    }
    .build()

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Support 2-3 versions simultaneously
  • Deprecate old versions on timeline
  • Use CDN for APK/updates
  • API-as-backend vs backend-for-frontend

docs.title: Authentication security
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Authentication proves identity. Securely integrating auth into mobile is critical for production systems.

docs.title: JWT (JSON Web Tokens)
docs.text:
Structure: header.payload.signature

Contains: - exp: expiration timestamp - sub: subject (user ID) - iat: issued at time - custom claims

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 for Mobile
docs.text:
Authorization code flow (for third-party login):

  1. App opens browser to provider
  2. User grants permission
  3. Provider sends authorization code
  4. App exchanges code for token
  5. App can now access resources

docs.title: Secure Token Storage
docs.text:
Never hardcode or store in plain SharedPreferences:

// Use EncryptedSharedPreferences
val encryptedPrefs = EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
    context,
    "secret",
    MasterKey.Builder(context).build(),
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
)

encryptedPrefs.edit().putString("auth_token", token).commit()

docs.title: Token Refresh Flow
docs.text:
When token expires:

class TokenRefreshingInterceptor : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        val response = chain.proceed(chain.request())

        if (response.code == 401) {
            synchronized(this) {
                val newToken = refreshToken()
                response.close()
                return chain.proceed(addToken(chain.request(), newToken))
            }
        }
        return response
    }
}

docs.title: Request/Response Flow
docs.text:
1. User logs in with credentials
  2. Server validates, returns tokens
  3. Access token stored securely
  4. Refresh token stored separately (longer TTL)
  5. All requests include access token
  6. On 401, refresh flow triggered

docs.title: JWT Token Structure
docs.text:
// Manually decode (never verify without server)
val parts = token.split(".")
val payload = String(Base64.getDecoder().decode(parts[1]))
// {"sub":"user123","exp":1640000000,"iat":1640000000}

docs.title: OkHttp Auth Interceptor
docs.text:
class AuthInterceptor(tokenProvider: TokenProvider) : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        val originalRequest = chain.request()
        val token = tokenProvider.getToken()

        val authenticatedRequest = originalRequest.newBuilder()
            .addHeader("Authorization", "Bearer $token")
            .build()

        return chain.proceed(authenticatedRequest)
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
Q: Should tokens be refreshed proactively? A: Yes, refresh shortly before expiration to avoid race conditions.

Q: Can JWT be revoked? A: Client can't know. Server maintains blacklist or uses short TTL.

Q: Is PKCE required for mobile? A: Yes for OAuth. Mobile can't keep secrets, so code challenge/verifier used.

docs.title: Token Lifetimes
docs.text:
• Access: 15-60 min (short, limited damage if leaked)
  • Refresh: 7-30 days (enables long sessions)
  • ID token (if OAuth): short like access

docs.title: Multi-Account Support
docs.text:
Some apps support multiple accounts:

// Store tokens per user ID
val userTokens = mapOf(
    "user1" -> token1,
    "user2" -> token2
)

fun selectAccount(userId: String) {
    currentToken = userTokens[userId]
}

docs.title: Cache Tokens in Memory
docs.text:
Avoid repeated disk access:

private var tokenCache: String? = null
private var cacheTime: Long = 0

fun getToken(): String {
    if (System.currentTimeMillis() - cacheTime < 5000) {
        return tokenCache!!  // recent cache
    }
    tokenCache = loadFromDisk()
    cacheTime = System.currentTimeMillis()
    return tokenCache!!
}

docs.title: Device Binding for Security
docs.text:
Link tokens to device to prevent theft:

val deviceId = Settings.Secure.getString(
    context.contentResolver,
    Settings.Secure.ANDROID_ID
)

// Include in token or sign with device key

docs.title: Biometric Integration
docs.text:
Protect token access with fingerprint/face:

BiometricPrompt(this, executor, callback).authenticate(promptInfo)
// Only on success do we unlock token

docs.title: Caching strategies
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: HTTP caching reduces bandwidth and latency.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Cache-Control header values: - max-age=300: cache 5 minutes - no-cache: revalidate always - no-store: never cache - private/public: for CDN

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// OkHttp automatic caching
val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .cache(Cache(cacheDir, 10L * 1024 * 1024))  // 10MB
    .build()

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Respect server Cache-Control headers
  • Use ETags for validation
  • Offline fallback: serve stale cache on error

docs.title: Certificate pinning
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Certificate pinning roots trust in specific server certificates, preventing MITM attacks via compromised CAs.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
CertificatePinner pins SHA-256 hashes of certificates: 

CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("example.com", "sha256/AAAA...")
    .add("*.example.com", "sha256/BBBB...")
    .build()

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val pinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/47DEQpj8HBSa...")
    .build()
val httpClient = OkHttp.Builder()
    .certificatePinner(pinner)
    .build()

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Pin multiple hashes for failover
  • Update hashes when certificates rotate
  • Handle pin failures gracefully (log, but allow optional bypass for dev)

docs.title: Compression optimization
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Compression (gzip, brotli) reduces bandwidth.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Accept-Encoding request header
  • Content-Encoding response header
  • OkHttp handles automatically
  • Saves ~60-80% bandwidth

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// Already transparent in OkHttp
val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addNetworkInterceptor { chain ->
        val response = chain.proceed(chain.request())
        // OkHttp automatically decompresses
        response
    }
    .build()

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Compression trade-off: CPU vs bandwidth
  • For images: compress beforehand (WebP, HEIC)
  • Disable for pre-compressed (videos)

docs.title: Conflict resolution
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: When local and remote changes conflict, determine winner.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Strategies: - Last-write-wins (simplest, timestamp-based) - Remote-wins (server authority) - Merge (combine non-conflicting fields) - Manual (show UI)

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// Last-write-wins merge
fun mergeUser(local: User, remote: User): User {
    return if (local.modifiedAt > remote.modifiedAt) {
        local
    } else {
        remote
    }
}
// Merge fields
fun mergeUser(local: User, remote: User): User {
    return User(
        id = remote.id,
        name = remote.name ?: local.name,
        email = local.email,  // prefer local
        modifiedAt = maxOf(local.modifiedAt, remote.modifiedAt)
    )
}

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Log conflicts for analytics
  • Version vectors for causal ordering
  • Expose unresolved conflicts in UI

docs.title: Error handling resilience
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Network errors are inevitable. Handle gracefully.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Error categories: - No connectivity (offline) - Timeout - 4xx client error (retry-safe: only 429) - 5xx server error (retry-safe) - Parse error (non-retriable)

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// Error classification
sealed class Result<T> {
    data class Success<T>(val data: T) : Result<T>()
    data class NetworkError<T>(val ex: IOException) : Result<T>()
    data class HttpError<T>(val code: Int) : Result<T>()
    data class ParseError<T>(val ex: Exception) : Result<T>()
}
// Retry decision
fun shouldRetry(result: Result<*>): Boolean {
    return result is Result.NetworkError || 
           result is Result.HttpError && result.code >= 500
}

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Classify errors for metrics
  • Fallback to cached data
  • Expose errors to user appropriately

docs.title: Graphql advanced
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: GraphQL vs REST trade-offs + gRPC alternatives.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: REST: - Resource-oriented - Fixed response shapes - Over/under-fetching common GraphQL: - Query language - Client specifies fields - Reduces bandwidth - Learning curve gRPC: - Binary protocol (faster) - Protocol Buffers schemas - Streaming support - Less browser-friendly

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// Apollo Kotlin for GraphQL
val apolloClient = ApolloClient.Builder()
    .serverUrl("https://api.example.com/graphql")
    .build()
// Query
val query = GetUserQuery(id = "123")
val response = apolloClient.query(query).execute()

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• GraphQL best for complex queries
  • gRPC for services/microservices
  • REST for simple CRUD

docs.title: Multipart uploads
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Multipart requests handle mixed binary/text data.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Use @Multipart @Part annotations in Retrofit.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
@Multipart
@POST("upload")
suspend fun uploadFile(
    @Part("description") description: RequestBody,
    @Part file: MultipartBody.Part
): Response
// Usage
val file = File(path)
val requestBody = file.asRequestBody("image/jpeg".toMediaType())
val part = MultipartBody.Part.createFormData("file", file.name, requestBody)
val description = "My image".toRequestBody("text/plain".toMediaType())
api.uploadFile(description, part)

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Chunk large files
  • Implement upload progress
  • Resume capability for large uploads

docs.title: Network monitoring debugging
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Monitor and debug network traffic in production and development.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Tools: - OkHttp logging interceptor - Android Studio Network Profiler - Chucker (in-app interceptor) - Stetho (Chrome debugging)

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val logging = HttpLoggingInterceptor().apply {
    level = HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.BODY
}
val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addNetworkInterceptor(logging)
    .build()

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Disable verbose logging in production
  • Use sampling for high-traffic
  • Correlate requests with metrics/tracing

docs.title: Offline first architecture
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Offline-first: local DB is source of truth, sync when connected.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
1. All reads from local DB
  2. Writes queued, synced
  3. Conflict resolution on sync
  4. Seamless online/offline

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// Room as local source
@Dao
interface UserDao {
    @Insert(onConflict = OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE)
    suspend fun insertUser(user: User)
    @Query("SELECT * FROM users")
    fun getAllUsers(): Flow<List<User>>
}
// Repository coordinates
class UserRepository(
    private val api: UserApi,
    private val dao: UserDao
) {
    fun getUsers(): Flow<List<User>> = dao.getAllUsers()
    suspend fun syncUsers() {
        val remote = api.listUsers()
        dao.insertAll(remote)
    }
}

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• WorkManager for background sync
  • Prioritize recent changes
  • Handle partial sync failures

docs.title: Okhttp internals
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: OkHttp is the HTTP client layer that Retrofit delegates to. Understanding OkHttp's architecture is critical for production networking engineering on Android.

docs.title: Request/Response Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Application creates Request
  2. Interceptor chain processes
  3. Connection pool consulted
  4. TCP connection established or reused
  5. TLS handshake if HTTPS
  6. HTTP request sent
  7. Response received and parsed
  8. Interceptor chain (response phase)
  9. Response returned to caller

docs.title: Interceptor Chain Architecture
docs.text:
OkHttp maintains two interceptor chains:

Application Interceptors: - See only your application's original request - Not called for retries or redirects - Perfect for logging, auth injection - Can short-circuit (return cached response)

Network Interceptors: - See actual network traffic including redirects - final response before actual network call - Can measure real latency - for debugging actual HTTP

docs.title: Connection Pooling
docs.text:
OkHttp reuses connections via a pool:

OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectionPool(ConnectionPool(
        maxIdleConnections = 5,
        keepAliveDuration = 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES
    ))
    .build()

Pool keyed by: host:port:scheme

Benefits: - reduces TLS handshakes - improves throughput - reduces battery usage

docs.title: Call Mechanics
docs.text:
Under the hood, synchronous Call:

interface Call <T> {
    fun execute(): Response<T>  // blocking
    fun enqueue(callback: Callback<T>)  // async
    fun clone(): Call<T>
    fun cancel()
}

Retrofit adapters convert this to suspend or Flow.

docs.title: Request Path
docs.text:
1. Application calls retrofit.userService.getUser(1)
  2. Proxy method intercepts via dynamic code gen
  3. RequestBuilder creates HTTP request
  4. Retrofit passes to OkHttp Call
  5. Application interceptors run
  6. Connection pool consulted
  7. If new connection: DNS → TCP → TLS
  8. Request written to socket
  9. Network interceptors run
  10. Response read from socket
  11. Converter deserializes JSON to object

docs.title: Response Path (Reverse)
docs.text: Response flows back through interceptors in reverse (post-processing).

docs.title: Custom Application Interceptor (Auth)
docs.text:
class AuthInterceptor : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        val original = chain.request()
        val token = getToken()  // from storage

        val authenticated = original.newBuilder()
            .addHeader("Authorization", "Bearer $token")
            .build()

        return chain.proceed(authenticated)
    }
}

val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor())
    .build()

docs.title: Retry Interceptor
docs.text:
class RetryInterceptor : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        var request = chain.request()
        var exception: IOException? = null

        repeat(3) { attempt ->
            try {
                return chain.proceed(request)
            } catch (e: IOException) {
                exception = e
                Thread.sleep(100L * (2.0).pow(attempt.toDouble()).toLong())
            }
        }

        throw exception ?: IOException("retry failed")
    }
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
Q: Why does OkHttp cache connections? A: TLS handshakes are expensive (~100ms each). Reusing connections amortizes that cost.

Q: What's the difference between application and network interceptors? A: Application interceptors see redirects as one flow. Network interceptors see each redirect as separate call.

Q: Can you short-circuit OkHttp? A: Yes, via application interceptor returning a cached response without calling chain.proceed().

docs.title: Timeouts Are Essential
docs.text:
OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .readTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .writeTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .callTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS)  // includes retries
    .build()

Missing timeouts = potential ANRs on network hang.

docs.title: Connection Pool Size
docs.text:
Default: 5 idle connections, 5 minute keep-alive.

For high-throughput apps, increase: 

ConnectionPool(maxIdleConnections = 10, keepAliveDuration = 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)

docs.title: DNS Caching
docs.text:
OkHttp doesn't cache DNS by default. For production reliability:

class HostnameVerifier : HostnameVerifier {
    private val systemVerifier = HttpsURLConnection.getDefaultHostnameVerifier()

    override fun verify(hostname: String, session: SSLSession) =
        systemVerifier.verify(hostname, session)
}

docs.title: Interceptor overhead
docs.text: Each interceptor adds slight latency. Minimize number of interceptors.

docs.title: Connection reuse > new connections
docs.text:
• New connection: ~150-300ms (TLS on 4G)
  • Reused connection: ~5-10ms

Massive difference on recursive API calls.

docs.title: Memory usage
docs.text: Connection pools consume memory. Monitor: - active connections - idle connections - buffer sizes

docs.title: Interceptor Composition
docs.text:
Multiple interceptors should be independent and composable:

// Anti-pattern: Logging depends on auth
interceptor1 = AuthInterceptor()
interceptor2 = LoggingInterceptor()  // assumes auth token present

// Better: Logging logs whatever headers exist

docs.title: Chunked Encoding
docs.text:
For streaming uploads, use RequestBody:

val body = object : RequestBody() {
    override fun contentType() = MediaType.parse("text/plain")

    override fun writeTo(sink: BufferedSink) {
        // Stream directly, no buffer
        for (chunk in dataStream) {
            sink.write(chunk)
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Connection Pool Lifecycle
docs.text:
OkHttp connection thread pool lives for entire app:

// Single shared instance (correct)
val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectionPool(ConnectionPool())
    .build()

// Within Retrofit
val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder()
    .client(httpClient)
    .build()

Creating new OkHttp clients = new thread pools = memory leak.

docs.title: Pagination architecture
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Pagination splits large results into manageable pages for mobile.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Approaches: 1. Offset/Limit: Simple, page shifts with inserts 2. Cursor: Opaque token, handles concurrent inserts 3. Keyset: Last ID, maintains ordering

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// Paging 3 integration
class UserPagingSource : PagingSource<Int, User>() {
    override suspend fun load(params: LoadParams<Int>): LoadResult<Int, User> {
        val page = params.key ?: 1
        val users = api.listUsers(page, params.loadSize)
        return LoadResult.Page(
            data = users,
            prevKey = if (page > 1) page - 1 else null,
            nextKey = page + 1
        )
    }
}
val pager = Pager(PagingConfig(pageSize = 20)) {
    UserPagingSource()
}
val flow = pager.flow.cachedIn(viewModelScope)

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Cursor-based prevents duplicates
  • Handle concurrent updates
  • Cache pages locally where possible

docs.title: Production networking patterns
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Production patterns: timeouts, security config, monitoring.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Timeouts prevent indefinite waits: - connectTimeout: 10-30s - readTimeout: 20-60s - writeTimeout: 20-60s - callTimeout: includes retries

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val httpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .readTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .writeTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .callTimeout(120, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .build()
// Network Security Config XML
<domain-config>
    <domain includeSubdomains="true">example.com</domain>
    <pin-set>
        <pin digest="SHA-256">...</pin>
    </pin-set>
</domain-config>

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• One OkHttp instance per app
  • Connection pool management
  • Timeouts must account for network latency
  • Production monitoring: latency, errors, bandwidth

docs.title: Rate limiting idempotency
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Rate limits prevent abuse. Idempotency enables safe retries.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: Rate limit headers: - X-RateLimit-Limit - X-RateLimit-Remaining - X-RateLimit-Reset - Retry-After Idempotency-Key: UUID for deduplication

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// Add Idempotency-Key to POST
val requestBody = RequestBody.create(...) 
val request = Request.Builder()
    .post(requestBody)
    .addHeader("Idempotency-Key", UUID.randomUUID().toString())
    .build()

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Respect rate limits (back off exponentially)
  • Per-user vs global limits
  • Circuit breaker on repeated 429s

docs.title: Rest api principles
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for distributed systems communication. Understanding REST principles is foundational for mobile networking.

docs.title: Six REST Constraints
docs.text:
1. Client-Server: UI separate from data storage
  2. Stateless: Each request contains all needed context
  3. Cacheable: Responses marked as cacheable/non-cacheable
  4. Uniform Interface: Consistent resource identification
  5. Layered System: Client can't tell if connected to end server
  6. Code on Demand: Optional; servers can extend client functionality

docs.title: Resource-Oriented Design
docs.text:
REST is resource-oriented, not action-oriented:

Wrong (RPC-style):
/getUser?id=123
/deleteUser?id=123
/updateUser?id=123&name=John

Right (REST):
GET /users/123
DELETE /users/123
PUT /users/123

Resources are nouns. HTTP methods are verbs.

docs.title: HTTP Status Codes
docs.text:
2xx (Success): - 200 OK: request succeeded - 201 Created: resource created - 204 No Content: success, no body

3xx (Redirect): - 301 Moved Permanently: resource moved - 304 Not Modified: cached response valid

4xx (Client Error): - 400 Bad Request: invalid request - 401 Unauthorized: authentication required - 403 Forbidden: authentication OK, but no permission - 404 Not Found: resource doesn't exist - 429 Too Many Requests: rate limited

5xx (Server Error): - 500 Internal Server Error: server broke - 503 Service Unavailable: temporarily down

docs.title: URL Structure
docs.text:
https://api.example.com/v1/users/123/posts
|_____________________________|  |||||
        Authority             Path segments

Path design:

/users/:id           # GET one, POST new, DELETE one
/users               # GET list, POST new
/users/:id/posts     # nested resource

docs.title: Content Negotiation
docs.text:
Clients indicate desired format:

Accept: application/json
Accept: application/xml
Accept: text/plain

Server responds:

Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8

docs.title: Complete Request Example
docs.text:
GET /users/123 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer token123
Accept: application/json

docs.title: Complete Response Example
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: max-age=300
ETag: "abc123"

{
  "id": 123,
  "name": "John",
  "email": "john@example.com"
}

docs.title: Retrofit REST API Interface
docs.text:
interface UserApi {
    @GET("users")
    suspend fun listUsers(
        @Query("page") page: Int = 1,
        @Query("limit") limit: Int = 20
    ): Response<List<User>>

    @GET("users/{id}")
    suspend fun getUser(@Path("id") id: Int): User

    @POST("users")
    suspend fun createUser(@Body user: User): User

    @PUT("users/{id}")
    suspend fun updateUser(
        @Path("id") id: Int,
        @Body user: User
    ): User

    @DELETE("users/{id}")
    suspend fun deleteUser(@Path("id") id: Int)
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
Q: Is REST a standard or a style? A: It's an architectural style/constraint set, not a standard. HTTP is the standard.

Q: Should I cache POST requests? A: Generally no. POST is for creating, which should always hit server.

Q: What's idempotence in REST? A: Repeated calls have same effect as single call. GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent. POST is not.

docs.title: API Versioning
docs.text:
(1) URL path: /v1/users /v2/users
(2) Header: Accept: application/vnd.api+v2+json
(3) Query: /users?version=2

Best: separate versions entirely so can deprecate.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Server should communicate limits:

X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 999
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1631234567
Retry-After: 60

Client must respect these.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
For large result sets:

GET /users?page=1&limit=20
GET /users?page=2&limit=20

// Or cursor-based
GET /users?limit=20
GET /users?limit=20&cursor=abc123

docs.title: Bandwidth Optimization
docs.text:
• Use gzip compression
  • Only request needed fields (GraphQL advantages)
  • Pagination to avoid huge payloads

docs.title: Caching Strategy
docs.text:
GET /users/123
  Cache-Control: max-age=300  # cache 5 min
GET /users/123/posts
  Cache-Control: no-cache     # revalidate always
POST /users
  Cache-Control: private, no-cache  # don't cache

docs.title: HATEOAS (Hypermedia)
docs.text:
Advanced REST includes hypermedia links:

{
  "id": 123,
  "name": "John",
  "_links": {
    "self": {"href": "/users/123"},
    "posts": {"href": "/users/123/posts"},
    "friends": {"href": "/users/123/friends"}
  }
}

Enables client discovery without hardcoding URLs. Rarely used in Android but important concept.

docs.title: REST Maturity Levels
docs.text:
1. Level 0: RPC (action-based URLs)
  2. Level 1: Resource-oriented (URLs)
  3. Level 2: HTTP methods + status codes
  4. Level 3: Hypermedia (HATEOAS)

Most mobile APIs are Level 2. Level 3 more common in web.

docs.title: When REST Isn't Enough
docs.text:
• Real-time: use WebSockets
  • Complex queries: consider GraphQL
  • Binary data: gRPC
  • Event streams: Server-Sent Events

docs.title: Retrofit fundamentals
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This topic is essential for Android networking interviews because it combines robust API design, converter behavior, and coroutine execution over OkHttp.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Keep API contracts explicit and versioned.
  • Separate transport errors from domain errors.
  • Prefer deterministic request/response mapping.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
• Retrofit handles interface parsing and adapter wiring.
  • OkHttp performs connection management and interceptors.
  • Converters map payloads into stable models.

docs.title: Request/Response Flow
docs.text:
• Build request from endpoint + headers + body.
  • Execute call through interceptor chain.
  • Map HTTP response into success/error result types.

docs.title: Caching & Persistence
docs.text:
• Use HTTP cache directives where possible.
  • Persist critical data for offline reads.
  • Define stale-read and refresh strategy explicitly.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
interface UserApi {
    @GET("users")
    suspend fun users(): List<UserDto>
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• How do you structure API interfaces for long-term maintainability?
  • Where should retry and timeout logic live?
  • How do you expose failures to the UI layer?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Add telemetry around status codes and latency percentiles.
  • Guard against schema drift with robust parsing defaults.
  • Use idempotency where retries can duplicate side effects.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
• Reuse connections aggressively through OkHttp pooling.
  • Minimize payload size and serialization overhead.

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text: • Strong answers include migration strategy and backward compatibility policy.

docs.title: Retry exponential backoff
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Retry logic + exponential backoff handle transient failures without overwhelming servers.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Idempotent operations (GET, PUT, DELETE) can retry
  • Non-idempotent (POST create) need caution
  • Exponential backoff: 2^attempt * base + jitter

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// OkHttp retry interceptor
class RetryInterceptor : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        repeat(3) { attempt ->
            try {
                return chain.proceed(chain.request())
            } catch (e: IOException) {
                if (attempt == 2) throw
                Thread.sleep(100 * (2.0.pow(attempt.toDouble())).toLong())
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Jitter prevents thundering herd
  • Set max total time, not just attempts
  • Backoff: connect > read > write timeouts

docs.title: Serialization strategies
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Serialization converts Kotlin objects to/from JSON. Performance and flexibility vary across libraries.

docs.title: Serialization Libraries
docs.text:
Gson (Google): - Reflection-based - Flexible, lenient parsing - No compile-time checks - mature, widely used

Moshi (Square): - Reflection + type adapters - Customizable parsing - Better error messages - faster than Gson

Kotlin Serialization (JetBrains): - Compiler plugin generates code - No reflection needed - Compile-time safety - Newer, growing adoption

docs.title: Gson vs Moshi vs Kotlin Serialization Comparison
docs.text: Aspect Gson Moshi Kotlin Serialization Speed 250μs 150μs 50μs Reflection Yes Partial No Type Safety Runtime Runtime Compile-time Error Messages Good Excellent Good Setup Easy Medium Medium

docs.title: Request/Response Flow
docs.text:
1. OkHttp receives response bytes
  2. Retrofit converter deserializes
  3. Object passed to collecting flow/callback

docs.title: Custom Gson Serializer
docs.text:
data class User(val id: Int, val createdAt: Date)

class DateSerializer : JsonSerializer<Date>,
    JsonDeserializer<Date> {
    private val fmt = SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd")

    override fun serialize(src: Date?, typeOfSrc: Type?,
        context: JsonSerializationContext?) = JsonPrimitive(fmt.format(src))

    override fun deserialize(json: JsonElement?, typeOfT: Type?,
        context: JsonDeserializationContext?) = 
        fmt.parse(json?.asString ?: "")
}

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
Q: Why is Kotlin Serialization faster? A: Compiler generates code instead of using reflection at runtime.

Q: Should I migrate from Gson? A: Only if performance is critical. Gson ecosystem is larger.

docs.title: Backwards Compatibility
docs.text:
When API adds fields:

@Serializable
data class User(
    val id: Int,
    val name: String,
    @Transient  // skip serialization
    val newFeature: String = "default"
)

docs.title: Caching Serializers
docs.text:
Create serializers once:

val gson = GsonBuilder()
    .registerTypeAdapter(...)
    .build()

// reuse
val user = gson.fromJson(json, User::class.java)

docs.title: Version Stability
docs.text:
Track API schema versions:

// v1 field removed, v2 added
if (apiVersion >= 2) {
    useNewField()
}

docs.title: Websockets streaming
docs.text: ← Back to Networking

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: WebSockets enable real-time bidirectional communication.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Full-duplex (both directions simultaneously)
  • Persistent connection
  • Low latency vs polling

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
// OkHttp WebSocket
val webSocket = httpClient.newWebSocket(
    Request.Builder().url("wss://echo.websocket.org").build(),
    object : WebSocketListener() {
        override fun onMessage(s: WebSocket, text: String) {
            println("Received: $text")
        }
        override fun onFailure(w: WebSocket, t: Throwable, r: Response?) {
            t.printStackTrace()
        }
    }
)
webSocket.send("Hello")

docs.title: Senior-Level Insights
docs.text:
• Reconnection logic essential
  • Heartbeat/ping-pong for keep-alive
  • Handle graceful disconnect

docs.title: Allocation optimization
docs.text: ← Back to Performance

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This topic matters in Android interviews because performance work requires object lifetime reduction, string/allocation control, and pooling where justified rather than guesswork.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Measure before optimizing.
  • Focus on user-visible latency and stability.
  • Keep regressions detectable through budgets.

docs.title: Internal Implementation
docs.text:
• Identify critical path in UI, data, and background work.
  • Isolate expensive operations away from the main thread.
  • Use bounded concurrency to reduce contention.

docs.title: Measurement and Profiling Flow
docs.text:
• Reproduce issue with a stable scenario.
  • Capture traces/profiles across CPU, memory, and rendering.
  • Validate fix with before/after metrics under same conditions.

docs.title: Optimization Techniques
docs.text:
• Remove unnecessary work first.
  • Reduce allocation and synchronization pressure.
  • Stage rollouts with monitoring guardrails.

docs.title: Code Examples
docs.text:
val start = System.nanoTime()
renderFrame()
val ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000.0

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
• Which metric tells you this optimization worked?
  • How do you avoid premature optimization?
  • What tradeoff did you accept to improve responsiveness?

docs.title: Production Considerations
docs.text:
• Define performance budgets per critical user journey.
  • Alert on regressions, not just absolute incidents.
  • Track low-end device behavior separately.

docs.title: Performance Insights
docs.text:
• Most wins come from reducing work, not micro-optimizations.
  • Smoothness consistency often matters more than peak throughput.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This topic is central to system design interviews because it forces explicit choices about ingestion design, batch vs stream, and data quality checks.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Define success metrics before proposing infrastructure.
  • Connect architecture choices to latency, reliability, and cost.
  • Keep rollback and migration strategy visible in the design.

docs.title: Internal Architecture
docs.text:
• Separate control plane concerns from request-serving paths.
  • Isolate heavy or failure-prone processing behind async boundaries.
  • Keep ownership boundaries aligned with team structure.

docs.title: Data and Request Flow
docs.text:
• Document request flow from ingress to persistence.
  • Identify where state is source-of-truth vs derived.
  • Make retry, dedupe, and idempotency behavior explicit.

docs.title: Scalability and Reliability
docs.text:
• Use bounded concurrency and backpressure at choke points.
  • Add timeouts, retries with jitter, and fail-fast guards.
  • Measure saturation signals and scale before user impact.
